text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, the elapsed time between consecutive completion events of A23 and A24 averaged about 1.0 hour (median about 1.0 hour, middle half roughly 0.9–1.1 hours); in the later window it averaged about 2.0 hours (median about 2.0 hours, middle half roughly 1.8–2.2 hours) — roughly a doubling, with the spread also widening (standard deviation about 0.17 → 0.35 hours) [TWAIT001].
- This gap was measured in all 200 traces of each window, and the difference is larger than in about 999.5 out of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data; note that this indicator measures elapsed time between consecutive completions, not pure waiting or service time [TWAIT001].
- Screening found no control-flow differences at the configured thresholds (0 of 55 tested units, against roughly 0.27 expected by chance); in the time family, 1 of 14 units qualified against roughly 0.007 expected by chance, so a single qualifying item is what an unchanged process can still occasionally produce [TWAIT001].

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence

The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process. The only sign of a difference is a single time item — the A23→A24 completion gap roughly doubling — in a family where about 0.007 items were expected by chance, so one qualifying item is what a stable process can still produce, and no structural or relational evidence corroborates it [TWAIT001].

Screening: 69 units tested, 0.28 items expected without change. By family:
- Control flow: 55 units tested, 0 items, 0.27 expected without change.
- Time: 14 units tested, 1 item, 0.007 expected without change.

So the time family has 1 item when 0.007 expected. Is 1 item "many times larger" than 0.007? The guidance says: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

Hmm, this is tricky. The expectation is 0.007, and we have 1 item. The example says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is what an unchanged process typically produces. 0.007 is fewer than one. So 1 item when 0.007 is expected... The example explicitly says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" → insufficient evidence. So even though 1/0.007 ≈ 143x, the rule says a single item when fewer than one is expected is what an unchanged process typically produces. Wait, but that seems contradictory: 1 item vs 0.007 expected is a count many times larger. Let me re-read.

"First compare the number of evidence items with the number expected by chance, per family when `screening.by_family` is present... A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks. A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole..."

So the example clarifies: one or two items when fewer than one is expected → same order → insufficient evidence. Here we have exactly 1 item in the time family when 0.007 is expected. That's "one item when fewer than one is expected" → insufficient evidence, "however large or unusual a single item looks."

So the verdict is Insufficient evidence. The single TWAIT item, however striking (mean elapsed time between consecutive completions of A23→A24 roughly doubled from ~1.0h to ~2.0h, empirical strength 0.9995), is a single item, and the screening expectation for the time family is 0.007... Hmm, but wait. Let me think again. The rule says "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole". 1 vs 0.007 is 143x. But the example explicitly overrides: "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is same order. The example seems designed exactly for this case: a single item with a tiny expectation. The phrase "however large or unusual a single item looks" strongly suggests that a single item, even with high empirical strength, should lead to insufficient evidence when the expectation is below one.

Actually, let me reconsider. The "same order" language: 0.007 and 1 are not the same order of magnitude mathematically. But the parenthetical example explicitly says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" counts as same order. So the intended reading: with integer counts, 1 or 2 items when expectation < 1 is typical of an unchanged process. So insufficient evidence.

Also control flow: 0 items when 0.27 expected — nothing there.

So: Support level: Insufficient evidence.

Observed differences: The only qualifying item is TWAIT001: elapsed time between consecutive completion events of A23 and A24 (the pair A23→A24). Before: mean ~1.0 hours, median ~1.0, IQR ~0.88–1.12. After: mean ~2.0 hours, median ~1.98, IQR ~1.76–2.23. So the gap roughly doubled. Support: 200 traces in each window (all traces). Empirical strength 0.9995 — the difference is larger than in ~999.5 of 2000 random re-splits. But this is a single item from the time family where ~0.007 items would qualify by chance; a single item is what an unchanged process can still produce occasionally. Also note TWAIT is elapsed time between consecutive completion events, not pure waiting/service time.

Also note: no control-flow items qualified (0 of 55 units, 0.27 expected), so no structural differences at thresholds.

Inference: Insufficient evidence. "The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process." Add one short sentence on limitation: a single time item (TWAIT001) with a doubled A23→A24 gap is unusual but a lone qualifying item is within what an unchanged process can produce at these thresholds; no structural evidence corroborates it.

No hypothesis stated. But should I mention the TWAIT observation? The observed differences section covers it. In the inference, one short sentence on limitation is allowed.

Every bullet/paragraph stating a fact about the data or a hypothesis must end with exactly one pair of square brackets listing supporting evidence identifiers. Actually I could write: "Screening found no control-flow differences (0 of 55 units vs about 0.27 expected) and a single time item (vs about 0.007 expected) [TWAIT001]." That works — the single time item is TWAIT001.

- In the earlier window, the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A23 and A24 (within-trace, consecutive events) averaged about 1.0 hour (median about 1.0 hour, middle half roughly 0.9–1.1 hours); in the later window it averaged about 2.0 hours (median about 2.0, middle half roughly 1.8–2.2), roughly a doubling, and the spread also grew (std ~0.17 → ~0.35 hours) [TWAIT001].

That's one sentence of limitation. Good.

The only sign of change is a single time item — the A23→A24 completion gap roughly doubling — in a family where about 0.007 items were expected by chance, so one qualifying item is what an unchanged process can still produce, and no structural evidence corroborates it [TWAIT001].

Good.

Also in observed differences, avoid saying "the process was changed to" — use "in the later window". Also mention earlier window state. Done.

Rounded percentages: "about 999.5 in 1000" — better "larger than in about 999.5 of 1000 random re-splits" or "in more than 999 of 1000". Use simple fractions: "larger than in about 9995 of 10000"? Simpler: "larger than in roughly 999.5 out of 1000 random re-splits". Fine.

Also note mean occurrences vs share of traces — not relevant here. TWAIT support is 200/200 traces in each window (count 200 components each). Actually support before/after = 200 each, and components count = 200 each. So the pair A23→A24 within five steps occurred in all 200 traces? LAG support definition: "traces containing the ordered pair within five steps for LAG". TWAIT is between consecutive completion events; support 200 in both windows. So the gap is measured 200 times per window. I can say "measured in all 200 traces of each window" — that's supported by support fields and component counts [TWAIT001].

One nuance: TWAIT analysis_unit values are ["A23","A24"] — the pair. The indicator is elapsed time between consecutive completion events. I'll describe it as "the elapsed time from the completion of A23 to the completion of the next event, A24" — actually it's between consecutive completion events of the pair A23 and A24. I'll say "between consecutive completions of A23 and A24".

Also should I avoid calling it "waiting time"? Yes — "do not call it pure waiting, service or processing time". I'll call it "elapsed time between consecutive completion events".

Also the observed_change ~0.99 hours on the hours scale.

Final check on sections and formatting. Two sections only. Bullets with citations. Keep concise.
